September 24, 2026 Updated October 3, 2026

**Court**: 9th Cir.
**Decided**: September 24, 2026
**Case No.**: 24-7282

PeaceHealth*, the Ninth Circuit reversed the dismissal of a nurse’s religious discrimination suit, holding that the trial court should have considered her religious exemption letter under the incorporation-by-reference doctrine—and that, once considered, her complaint plausibly pleaded a Title VII failure-to-accommodate claim. November 11, 2026

Volume XVI, Number 315

Nurse’s Religious Exemption Letter Should Have Been Considered On Motion To Dismiss

Wednesday, November 11, 2026

Ridings v. PeaceHealth, 2026 WL 2871881 (9th Cir. 2026)

Karly Ridings, a registered nurse who was pregnant at the relevant time, sent a letter to her employer (the PeaceHealth hospital system in Oregon) requesting a religious exemption from its COVID-19 vaccination policy, citing her Christian beliefs and her religious objection to the use of fetal cell lines derived from abortions in vaccine development. PeaceHealth placed her on indefinite unpaid leave without benefits during her third trimester. The district court dismissed her Title VII and state-law failure-to-accommodate claims without leave to amend, finding her complaint too conclusory because it did not attach or describe the exemption letter in detail. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the letter was incorporated by reference into the complaint because it was central to her claim and that, considering the letter, Ridings “easily satisfie[d]” the plausibility threshold for a prima facie religious discrimination claim.

# KARLY RIDINGS v. PEACEHEALTH (2026)
## United States Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit.
### COUNSEL Paul Janzen (argued) and Caroline Janzen, Rugged Law Inc, Portland, Oregon, for Plaintiff-Appellant. Michael T. Garone (argued), Kelly S. Riggs, and Megan Breen, Schwabe Williamson & Wyatt PC, Portland, Oregon, for Defendant-Appellee.
OPINION

Karly Ridings, a registered nurse at the PeaceHealth hospital system, objected to her employer's mandatory COVID-19 vaccination policy on religious grounds. In her letter seeking a religious accommodation, Ridings said that the vaccine derives from fetal cells and that the vaccination policy thus conflicts with her opposition to abortion rooted in her Christian faith. PeaceHealth responded by placing Ridings on indefinite, unpaid leave. Ridings then sued, claiming that the hospital failed to accommodate her religious beliefs under federal and state law. The district court apparently ignored Ridings' letter because it had not been attached to her complaint. It then dismissed the lawsuit without giving leave to amend, ruling that Ridings did not adequately explain the religious basis for objecting to the COVID-19 vaccine.

We hold that the district court erred in not considering Ridings' religious exemption request letter and then dismissing the complaint. Under the incorporation-by-reference doctrine, the district court should have considered the contents of Ridings' letter because it is central to her claim. And once we consider her letter, Ridings easily satisfies the plausibility threshold for a prima facie Title VII religious discrimination claim. Courts generally cannot question the sincerity of someone's religious beliefs: Judges may wear robes, but we are not men and women of cloth who can opine on religious convictions. We reverse the dismissal of the lawsuit.

[Justia Opinion Summary](https://connect.justia.com/case-law-summary-newsletters)
A registered nurse employed by a hospital system in Oregon requested a religious exemption from her employer’s mandatory COVID-19 vaccination policy. P. 12(b)(6) dismissal of Karly Ridings’s employment discrimination action against PeaceHealth, alleging a failure to accommodate her religious beliefs under Title VII and Oregon state law, and remanded for further proceedings. Ridings, a registered nurse, sent a letter to PeaceHealth requesting a religious exemption from a mandatory vaccination policy on two religious grounds. In response, PeaceHealth placed her on indefinite leave without benefits or pay.

The district court erred in dismissing Ridings’ complaint. We hold that the district court erred in not considering the contents of Ridings’ religious exemption letter in deciding the motion to dismiss. And if we consider the religious reasons set out in Ridings’ letter, she has plausibly alleged a prima facie case for a religious discrimination claim. A. Ridings’ religious exemption letter is central to her claim and thus was incorporated by reference into the complaint.

CONCLUSION We REVERSE the district court’s dismissal of Ridings’ claims for relief and REMAND for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Because the merits of Ridings’ case turned on the religious reasons stated in her letter, and her complaint referenced it while no party contested its authenticity, the court should have considered its contents.
The Holding
A religious exemption request letter that a failure-to-accommodate claim necessarily relies on is incorporated by reference into the complaint, and a court deciding a motion to dismiss should consider its contents even when the letter is not attached to the pleading.

Whether the Complaint Plausibly Pleaded a Religious Conflict

Considering the letter, the court held that Ridings plausibly alleged a bona fide religious belief that conflicted with the vaccination policy. Claims of religious discrimination need only meet the same plausibility standard as any other request for relief, and courts must be careful not to probe the sincerity or reasonableness of a claimant’s religious convictions.
The court distinguished its recent decision in Detwiler v. Mid-Columbia Medical Center , which requires a plaintiff to plead enough facts showing a belief is religious rather than purely secular. There, the objection to a nasal swab rested on a secular judgment that the swab was physically harmful. Here, Ridings’ letter stated with specificity that her faith bars using products derived from fetal cells made available through abortion, and she supported that objection with scripture.
Because Ridings sufficiently pleaded a religious objection based on the use of fetal cells, the court did not decide whether her other objections stated a claim. It reversed the dismissal and remanded for further proceedings.
What This Means for You
This decision confirms that a religious exemption letter central to a failure-to-accommodate claim may be considered on a motion to dismiss under the incorporation-by-reference doctrine, even when it is not attached to the complaint.

Ridings’ complaint referenced her exemption request but did not attach the letter or detail its contents. When PeaceHealth moved to dismiss, she attached the letter to her opposition and asked for leave to amend if the pleading was found insufficient.
Karly Ridings, a registered nurse at the PeaceHealth hospital system in Oregon, objected to her employer’s mandatory COVID-19 vaccination policy on religious grounds.
PeaceHealth responded by placing Ridings, then in her third trimester of pregnancy, on indefinite leave without benefits or pay.
